conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of your neurology team doctors. You're here today for your 18th cycle of maintenance chemotherapy with rituximab and high-dose methotrexate for your CNS lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Doctor. Yes, I’ve been doing this every four months now. I’m feeling okay, just still noticing those floaters in my vision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The floaters have been stable and less bothersome than before, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely better. No new headaches or weakness. I’ve been keeping track, just like you asked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll start with rituximab today, followed by the high-dose methotrexate. We’ll give you fluids and sodium bicarbonate to protect your kidneys, especially since you’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, the methotrexate did affect my kidneys once. Are we watching that closely again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll check your creatinine and electrolytes daily. We also monitor your methotrexate levels to make sure they come down safely with leucovorin rescue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver? Last time my enzymes went up a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw a mild transaminitis last cycle. We’ll keep an eye on your AST and ALT. It usually improves on its own, but we’ll track it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better. When will the infusion start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about an hour. The nurse will start your hydration and premedicate you before rituximab to prevent any reactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your rituximab infusion is going smoothly. We’re about halfway through, and your vital signs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel fine. No chills or itching. That’s a good sign, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. We’ll continue monitoring. After this, we’ll start the methotrexate, which will take a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, the methotrexate infusion is complete. You tolerated it well. We’ll keep you on fluids and sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize your urine and protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. When do I start the leucovorin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about 24 hours, and then every 6 hours after that, based on your methotrexate levels. We’ll draw blood tomorrow morning to check your level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll stay here until it’s safe to go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, usually about 4–5 days. We want to make sure your methotrexate level drops below 0.05 µM and your liver and kidney function are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are back. Your creatinine is stable at 0.9, which is great. Your AST is a bit elevated at 57, but it’s trending down from last cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s not too bad? It was higher before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. It peaked higher last time. This mild elevation is common with chemo and should resolve. Your methotrexate level is 0.18 µM today—coming down as expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And leucovorin is helping with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It rescues your healthy cells from methotrexate toxicity. We’ll keep giving it every 6 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been a bit tired, but no nausea or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fatigue is common. We’ll keep you comfortable. You’re doing well overall.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your methotrexate level is now 0.06 µM—great progress. Your AST is down to 48. Kidneys still stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I heard I’m getting an MRI today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, without contrast, to check for any changes in your brain lesions. It’s part of your routine monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it show if the lymphoma is still under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re looking for stability—no new lesions or growth. Given your response so far, we expect it to be stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. The MRI results are back. No new changes. The FLAIR hyperintensities in your brain are stable, and no new areas of concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So no sign of recurrence?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None. The report says no acute process and no new lesions. This is exactly what we hope to see.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I was a little anxious about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. You’re responding well to maintenance therapy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news: your methotrexate level is now less than 0.04 µM. That means it’s cleared enough for us to consider discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Any other tests today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they did a follow-up MRI with some contrast sequences today. Again, no abnormal enhancement—confirms no active tumor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So both MRIs agree—stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, completely. The small areas from before are unchanged. No enhancement means no active lymphoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a huge weight off my shoulders.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve earned it. You’re doing very well with this regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also gave you the seasonal flu vaccine this morning. It’s safe to get it during this window between chemo cycles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was wondering about that. I didn’t want to get sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. With your immune system, it’s important to stay protected. You should have good coverage now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your labs are stable, methotrexate is undetectable, and your MRI is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Any changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing your omeprazole from 40 mg twice daily to 20 mg twice daily. The rest stays the same: aspirin, nitroglycerin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel off—fever or nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your oncologist. If you have a fever over 101, chills, or vomiting, go to the ER. Otherwise, follow up in two weeks as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate how well you’ve all taken care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done great. Keep up the good work, and we’ll see you for your next cycle in four months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. The nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. The instructions are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Stay hydrated, watch for any unusual symptoms, and keep your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson. We’ll see you next time.
